# Everything ran, and the answer came out backwards

`Krt5` is a mouse gene, and across the 12 samples in this chapter its average
reads 2,728.5 counts per million in one cell type and 4.3 in the other. About
six hundredfold. The whole result turns on which cell type goes with which
number, and that comes out of a second file holding 12 rows of labels.

Line those two files up wrong and every number above stays the same. The counts
don't move and nothing errors. The two words swap places, and the answer
inverts. By the end of this chapter you'll know how to catch that in two
minutes, and why the largest signal in this dataset isn't the one most readers
arrive looking for.

<!-- nlr-allow: 2728 -->

## What this analysis is asking

[Differential expression]{.term def="Comparing one gene's counts between two
groups of samples, then repeating that comparison for every gene."} is one
question asked once per gene: is the average different between group A and
group B? Four things stand between a file of counts and an answer to it, and
every one of them moves the answer.

### A count is not an amount

A count is the number of sequencing reads that landed on one gene in one
sample. It belongs to the cell and to the depth of the sequencing run, both at
once. Sequence the same cells twice as deeply and every count roughly doubles,
so a gene at 100 counts in one sample and 120 in a deeper one may not have
moved. Divide each column by its own total and the depth cancels. Chapter 20
called the result counts per million.

### Two labels on the same 12 samples

Twelve samples, split two ways. Six came from basal cells and six from luminal
cells, which is the `cell_type` label. Four came from virgin mice, four from
pregnant mice and four from lactating mice, which is the `stage` label. Each
combination of the two holds exactly 2 samples.

So basal against luminal has 6 samples on each side, and virgin against
lactating inside one cell type has 2. The difference between 6 and 2 runs the
back half of this chapter.

::: {.why}
A mammary duct is built from two layers of cells. Luminal cells line the inside
and make the milk. Basal cells wrap around the outside and squeeze it out. The
two layers carry different keratin proteins, which is how anyone tells them
apart. Both sit in every one of these 12 samples, and neither changes across
pregnancy the way the other does.
:::

### Ratios need a log

The log axis in Chapter 21 was there for a reason. A gene that doubled sits at
2.0 and one that halved sits at 0.5, and those are the same size of move written
as two numbers that look nothing alike. Take a log base 2 and they become +1 and
-1. Every fold change in this chapter is a log2 fold change, so +1 means doubled
and -3 means down eightfold.

### Two numbers per gene, and the second one is the hard one

For each gene you get a log2 fold change, which is the difference between the
two group averages, and a p-value from a t-test. The p-value answers a narrow
question: if this gene really didn't differ between the groups, how often would
random noise hand me a gap this big?

You'll run that test 14,210 times before this chapter is out, and at that scale
a p-value below 0.05 stops meaning much. The proper version of that argument is
Chapter 25's job. For now the pipeline also reports an adjusted p-value, and
the adjusted column is the one you read.

The t-test isn't what a working analyst would run on counts. DESeq2, published
by Michael I. Love, Wolfgang Huber and Simon Anders in 2014, and edgeR,
published by Mark D. Robinson, Davis J. McCarthy and Gordon K. Smyth in 2010,
both fit a negative binomial model instead, because a gene at 20 reads is
noisier than a gene at 2,000 in a way a t-test can't see. The pipeline below
runs a t-test anyway, out of parts you've already met apart from the
multiple-testing correction, and Chapter 25 says what that costs.

## Loading the counts

You should already have `data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz` and
`data/GSE60450_samples.csv` from Chapter 20, at 513,592 bytes and 526 bytes. If
either isn't sitting next to your notebook, fetch it before you run anything
here.

The count file is gzipped. In Chapter 20 you handed the file name straight to
pandas and let it unpack the file on the way in, which works. This version
unpacks it in a line of its own first, so the step is on the page rather than
implied, and both routes hand you the same table.

```{python}
import gzip
import io
import pandas as pd

raw = gzip.decompress(open("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", "rb").read())
counts = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(raw.decode()), sep="\t", index_col=0)
counts.pop("Length")
counts.columns = [name.split("_")[0] for name in counts.columns]

print(counts.shape)
print(" ".join(counts.columns[:6]))
print(" ".join(counts.columns[6:]))
```

`counts.pop("Length")` removes the gene-length column, for the reason Chapter 21
gave: it isn't a sample, and it would get averaged as though it were one. The
line after it cuts each column name down at the first underscore, because the
file ships names like `MCL1-DG_BC2CTUACXX_ACTTGA_L002_R1` and only the first
piece identifies the sample. The rest of it describes the sequencing run, not
the mouse.

The row labels are Entrez gene IDs, not symbols. `110308` is a stable
identifier and `Krt5` is a name that nomenclature committees are allowed to
change.

Now the library sizes.

```{python}
library_size = counts.sum()
print(library_size.min(), library_size.max())
print((library_size.max() / library_size.min()).round(3))
```

The deepest sample carries about 1.23 times the reads of the shallowest. Divide
each column by its own total and multiply by a million.

```{python}
cpm = counts / library_size * 1e6
keep = (cpm >= 1).sum(axis=1) >= 3
kept = counts.loc[keep]

print(counts.shape[0], "genes before filtering")
print(kept.shape[0], "genes after filtering")
```

Read the filter as a sentence. A gene stays if it reaches at least 1 count per
million in at least 3 of the 12 samples. A gene with 2 reads in one sample and
0 in the rest can't tell you anything, and it still consumes a test. Both
numbers are choices. Raise the sample count and you lose genes that switch on
in only one small group. Exercise 24.2 takes the filter away so you can watch
what it was doing.

::: {.check}
`counts` has 27,179 rows and `kept` has 14,210. If your second number is
27,179 as well, the filter didn't apply, and the usual cause is running the
cell that builds `keep` before the cell that builds `cpm`.
:::

A last transform, and then the table is ready to test.

```{python}
import numpy as np

logcpm = np.log2(kept / kept.sum() * 1e6 + 1)
print(logcpm.iloc[:3, :4].round(2))
```

The `+ 1` inside the log is the one Chapter 21 explained. It shifts a zero to a
log of zero and leaves large values essentially alone.

## Failure one: the labels

The labels live in a second file, one row per sample.

```{python}
samples = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_samples.csv").set_index("sample")
geo_order = samples.sort_values("gsm")
print(geo_order[["gsm", "cell_type", "stage"]])
```

Sort 12 accessions and that's the order you get. Six luminal samples, then six
basal ones, with virgin, pregnant and lactating appearing twice inside each
block.

::: {.asof}
Checked against GEO on 2 August 2026. This series carries one accession per
sample, `GSM1480291` through `GSM1480302`, and the counts arrive separately as
a file somebody uploaded. No step anywhere checks that the two orders agree.
:::

Twelve rows of metadata, 12 columns of counts. The obvious move is to staple
them together.

```{python}
wrong_labels = pd.DataFrame({
    "column": counts.columns,
    "gsm": geo_order["gsm"].values,
    "cell_type": geo_order["cell_type"].values,
    "stage": geo_order["stage"].values,
})
print(wrong_labels)
```

Look at that table. Twelve rows, no blanks and no repeats, six labeled luminal
and six labeled basal, two of each stage inside each. On paper the design is
flawless.

It is also wrong for all 12 samples.

Nothing you do next will tell you that. The samples really do fall into two
clean groups of six, and the principal component table below shows them doing
it. No plot has an opinion about labels. One column of one small table is
reversed, and it's the column your question rests on.

### The check that catches it

The table has no way to know what its columns contain, so you ask the data
instead, using a gene whose behavior you already know.

A [marker gene]{.term def="A gene whose expression is high in one cell type and
low in others, used to tell those cell types apart."} is a gene that's reliably
high in one cell type and low in another. Basal cells carry keratin 5 and
keratin 14, luminal cells carry keratin 8 and keratin 18. The mouse gene
`Krt5`, Entrez `110308`, should therefore read high in the basal samples and
low in the luminal ones.

Take that split on my word for one page, then check it without me on NCBI Gene
the way Chapter 5 taught you. If the record and this page disagree, believe the
record.

```{python}
krt5 = (kept.loc[110308] / kept.sum() * 1e6).round(1)
print(krt5)
```

Now split those 12 numbers by the labels you just attached.

```{python}
grouped = krt5.groupby(wrong_labels.set_index("column")["cell_type"])
print(grouped.mean().round(1))
```

`Krt5` comes out at 4.3 counts per million in the samples labeled basal and
2,728.5 in the samples labeled luminal. That is backwards, and it isn't close.
The gap runs about six hundredfold the wrong way.

::: {.trap}
The count matrix runs basal columns first, then luminal. The GEO accessions run
luminal first, then basal. Stapling one to the other by position gives all 12
samples the wrong cell type, and the stage labels stay correct, because both
orderings run virgin, pregnant, lactating inside their blocks. Nothing errors,
nothing is missing, and the design table looks textbook.
:::

Your first instinct on seeing those two group means will be to wonder whether
basal cells in this study somehow don't make `Krt5`. Reject it. The keratin
split is decades old and your join is four minutes old. When a marker gene says
your labels are backwards, your labels are backwards.

These 12 samples cost somebody months of animal work and a sequencing budget.
Your join cost you one line. Suspect the cheap thing first.

Do this before every comparison you ever run. Pick a gene whose answer you
already know, and confirm the data agrees before you ask it anything else. In
mammary tissue that gene is `Krt5`. Two minutes of that is what everything you
don't know sits on.

### Joining by key instead

The fix is one line, and it's the line Chapter 20 asked you to remember.

```{python}
samples = samples.loc[counts.columns]
print(samples[["gsm", "cell_type", "stage"]])
```

`samples.loc[counts.columns]` reorders the metadata rows to match the count
columns by name. If a name were missing, pandas would raise a `KeyError` and
you'd know. Positional stapling has no such protection. It lines up whatever
you hand it, silently, forever.

Run the marker check again on the repaired labels.

```{python}
print(krt5.groupby(samples["cell_type"]).mean().round(1))
```

The same 12 numbers, grouped a different way, and now `Krt5` points where the
biology says it should. A single line separates the wrong version of this
chapter from the right one, so write the join by key every time.

::: {.check}
`Krt5` should sit in the thousands of counts per million across all six basal
columns and in the single digits across all six luminal ones. If your two group
means come out the other way round, you're still on `wrong_labels`. Re-run the
cell that reassigns `samples`, then this one.
:::

## Failure two: the biggest thing in the table isn't your question

Labels fixed. Chapter 21 sorted these 12 samples with a principal component
plot. Here's the same analysis as four lines of arithmetic on `logcpm`, printed
as a table.

```{python}
centered = logcpm.T - logcpm.T.mean()
u, s, vt = np.linalg.svd(centered, full_matrices=False)
pcs = pd.DataFrame(u[:, :2] * s[:2], index=logcpm.columns,
                   columns=["PC1", "PC2"]).round(0).astype(int)
pcs["cell_type"] = samples["cell_type"]
pcs["stage"] = samples["stage"]

print(pcs)
print((s ** 2 / (s ** 2).sum() * 100).round(1)[:2])
```

PC1 accounts for 66.9 percent of the variation and it sorts the samples cleanly
into basal on one side and luminal on the other. PC2 holds 20.8 percent and it
tracks stage. The strongest signal in this dataset is cell type, whatever
question you arrived with.

Say your question is about lactation. You could pool the two cell types, put
all four virgin samples in one group and all four lactating samples in the
other, and test that. Lactation moves genes one way in basal cells and another
way in luminal ones, so pooling averages two different moves into one number
that belongs to neither. The results table won't tell you that. It carries one
fold change per gene and no column for which half of the tissue the number came
from. Exercise 24.1 puts a number on how far apart the two halves are.

Two fixes exist. The one this book can't teach you is a model carrying both
factors at once, which is what a line like `~ cell_type + stage` does in a
methods section. The one you can do today is to pick a cell type and stay
inside it. This chapter picks basal, which leaves 2 samples against 2, and the
rest of the chapter pays for that.

## Comparing basal against luminal

Start with the comparison the data is built for, because it's the one with 6
samples on each side.

```{python}
from scipy import stats

def benjamini_hochberg(p):
    n = len(p)
    order = np.argsort(p)
    ranked = p[order] * n / (np.arange(n) + 1)
    ranked = np.minimum.accumulate(ranked[::-1])[::-1]
    out = np.empty(n)
    out[order] = np.clip(ranked, 0, 1)
    return out

def compare(group_a, group_b):
    a = logcpm[group_a]
    b = logcpm[group_b]
    t, p = stats.ttest_ind(b, a, axis=1)
    table = pd.DataFrame({
        "log2_fold_change": b.mean(axis=1) - a.mean(axis=1),
        "p_value": p,
    }, index=logcpm.index)
    table = table.dropna(subset=["p_value"])
    table["p_adjusted"] = benjamini_hochberg(table["p_value"].values)
    return table.sort_values("p_value")

print(benjamini_hochberg(np.array([0.001, 0.02, 0.5])).round(4))
```

`stats.ttest_ind(b, a, axis=1)` runs one t-test per row, all 14,210 at once.
Argument order matters: `b` first means a positive fold change is higher in
group B. The `dropna` line has a trap box of its own below.

`benjamini_hochberg` is the one block in this chapter built out of numpy calls
this book never taught, and you don't have to read them to use it. Watch what it
does instead. The last line of that cell runs the correction on three made-up
p-values so you can see its shape. Feed it 0.001, 0.02 and 0.5 and you get back
0.003, 0.03 and 0.5. Each p-value is multiplied by the number of tests and
divided by its own position in the sorted list. The smallest is first of three,
so it goes up threefold. The largest comes back unchanged. Yoav Benjamini and
Yosef Hochberg published that arithmetic in 1995, and what it means is Chapter
25's argument.

```{python}
basal = samples.index[samples.cell_type == "basal"].tolist()
luminal = samples.index[samples.cell_type == "luminal"].tolist()
by_cell = compare(basal, luminal)

print(len(by_cell), "genes tested")
print((by_cell["p_value"] < 0.05).sum(), "with raw p below 0.05")
print((by_cell["p_adjusted"] < 0.05).sum(), "with adjusted p below 0.05")
print(by_cell["p_value"].median().round(4), "median p-value")
```

7,279 genes come in under a raw p of 0.05 and 6,199 of them survive
correction. That's 44 percent of the genes you tested, which sounds
implausible until you remember what you compared: two different cell types.

The median p-value is worth a look. When nothing is going on, p-values spread
evenly between 0 and 1 and the median sits near 0.5. This one is 0.0443. These
two groups of samples are not the same.

A list of 6,199 genes isn't an answer to anything, and you can't read it. You
can sort it and check whether the genes at the top are ones a mammary biologist
would expect there. Chapter 25 turns that move into a method. Now put names on
the strongest five.

```{python}
symbols = {12293: "Cacna2d1", 94088: "Trim6", 77220: "Tmem200a",
           110308: "Krt5", 594844: "Tceal3", 56461: "Kcnip3",
           109594: "Lmo1", 14663: "Glycam1", 67102: "D16Ertd472e",
           12189: "Brca1"}

top_cell = by_cell.head(5).copy()
top_cell["symbol"] = [symbols.get(gene, "") for gene in top_cell.index]
print(top_cell[["symbol", "log2_fold_change", "p_adjusted"]]
      .round({"log2_fold_change": 2}))
```

`Krt5` is fourth, at a log2 fold change of -8.97. Negative means lower in
luminal, and 2 to the power of 8.97 is a little over 500-fold. That's the gene
you used to catch the label error, arriving near the top of a list you built
without mentioning it.

## The question you came with

Inside the basal samples, 2 virgin against 2 lactating. `pick` pulls the sample
names for one cell type at one stage.

```{python}
def pick(cell_type, stage):
    return samples.index[(samples.cell_type == cell_type)
                         & (samples.stage == stage)].tolist()

by_stage = compare(pick("basal", "virgin"), pick("basal", "lactating"))

print(len(by_stage), "genes tested")
print((by_stage["p_value"] < 0.05).sum(), "with raw p below 0.05")
print((by_stage["p_adjusted"] < 0.05).sum(), "with adjusted p below 0.05")
print(by_stage["p_value"].median().round(4), "median p-value")
```

5,390 genes come in under a raw p of 0.05. Nine survive correction. Nine.

Nothing went wrong in that cell. Two mice per group is what this study
collected, and nine is what two mice per group buys, for anyone who runs it. A
longer list needs more mice, and that decision was made before the data
existed.

Four genes fewer went into this comparison than the last one: 14,210 minus 4 is
14,206. Those 4 had identical values inside both groups, which gives the t-test
nothing to divide by, so scipy returns `NaN` and the `dropna` line in `compare`
sets them aside.

::: {.trap}
Leave those four `NaN` values in and `np.minimum.accumulate` drags a `NaN`
backwards through the entire sorted list of adjusted p-values. Every one of the
14,210 becomes `NaN`. Then `(table["p_adjusted"] < 0.05).sum()` returns 0, no
error is raised, and you write down that nothing survived correction. That zero
is four broken rows reporting themselves as a finding.
:::

Put names on the strongest five here too.

```{python}
top_stage = by_stage.head(5).copy()
top_stage["symbol"] = [symbols.get(gene, "") for gene in top_stage.index]
print(top_stage[["symbol", "log2_fold_change", "p_adjusted"]].round(4))
```

The third row prints no symbol, because `symbols` only holds the ten genes this
chapter names. Entrez `68355` is a real gene with a real result, and NCBI Gene
will give it a name.

Nine genes out of 14,206, on a comparison holding 2 samples in each group, is
the honest version of what you have. A gene that missed the cut isn't a gene
that stayed still. With 2 against 2 you had almost no chance of showing that it
moved, and Chapter 25 works through what that does to a list this size.

## Brca1

You've been carrying this gene since Chapter 5. Here it is in your own results.

```{python}
for label, table in (("basal vs luminal", by_cell),
                     ("virgin vs lactating, basal", by_stage)):
    row = table.loc[12189]
    rank = int((table["p_value"] < row["p_value"]).sum()) + 1
    print(f"{label:28s} log2FC={row['log2_fold_change']:+.2f} "
          f"p={row['p_value']:.3g} p_adj={row['p_adjusted']:.3g} "
          f"rank={rank}")
```

Mouse *Brca1*, Entrez `12189`, in basal against luminal: a log2 fold change of
+1.96, a p-value of 0.00265, an adjusted p-value of 0.00914, rank 4,127. Higher
in luminal cells than basal ones, by a bit under fourfold.

In the comparison you actually came for, virgin against lactating inside the
basal samples, it moves the other way at -2.29 with a p-value of 0.00804. Its
adjusted p-value is 0.0693, so it sits above the 0.05 line and outside the nine
that survived. Rank 1,645 of 14,206.

The table says that much, and no more. *Brca1* peaks at 494 raw reads in its
best sample and bottoms out at 17. Counts that small can produce a large ratio
off very little evidence, which is where a raw p-value and an adjusted one part
company.

The study these samples came from wasn't about *Brca1* at all. Nai Yang Fu and
colleagues published it in *Nature Cell Biology* in 2015, working on a gene
called Mcl1, which is why every sample is named `MCL1-` something. The paper is
PubMed 25730472. *Brca1* turns up here because the sequencing covered every
gene in the mouse. That's a fact about the dataset, not a finding.

You now have two results tables in the notebook. `by_cell` holds 14,210 rows
comparing basal against luminal, sorted so the smallest p-value is on top.
`by_stage` holds 14,206 rows comparing virgin against lactating inside the
basal samples. Chapter 25 opens on those two and decides which rows are worth a
sentence.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="KeyError: \"['MCL1-DG'] not in index\""}
Pandas is talking, and it's talking about `samples.loc[counts.columns]`. One of
your count columns has no matching row in the metadata. Run
`print(list(counts.columns))` and `print(list(samples.index))` and read the two
lists side by side. If instead the message starts `None of [Index([` and then
prints long names full of underscores, you skipped the line that cuts each
column name at the first underscore.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: All arrays must be of the same length"}
You built `wrong_labels` from arrays that aren't all 12 long. The usual cause
is that `counts` still carries its `Length` column, so `counts.columns` has 13
entries against 12 rows of metadata.
:::

::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'Length'"}
`counts.pop("Length")` already ran and there's nothing left to remove. Running
a cell twice is normal and this is what it looks like. Restart the runtime and
run every cell from the top.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your p_adjusted column is entirely NaN"}
Python isn't complaining, which is why this one is dangerous. A single `NaN`
p-value propagates through `np.minimum.accumulate` and wipes out the whole
column. Check with `print(table['p_value'].isna().sum())`. If that's above
zero, you're missing the `dropna` line in `compare`.
:::
:::

- Join a sample table to a count matrix by key, and describe what a positional
  join does to this dataset
- Read a principal component table and name the factor that dominates it

- Find one named gene in a results table and report its log2 fold change and
